headings.title: Introduction and Normal Anatomy of the Placenta
headings.content: The placenta is a vital, temporary organ that facilitates nutrient, gas, and waste exchange between the mother and the developing fetus. In a normal human pregnancy, the placenta typically develops a discoid shape, measuring approximately 15 to 20 centimeters in diameter and weighing about 500 grams at term, which constitutes roughly one-sixth of the birth weight. Anatomically, it is divided into two primary surfaces: the fetal surface (chorionic plate), which is smooth, shiny, and covered by the amnion with the umbilical cord inserting near or at the center, and the maternal surface (basal plate), which is rough, spongy, and divided into 15 to 20 functional subdivisions known as cotyledons. Understanding this normal anatomy is crucial for nursing students in Nigeria and globally, as it forms the baseline for identifying structural variations and pathological conditions during the immediate postpartum inspection of the placenta. Following delivery, healthcare providers must meticulously examine both surfaces and the cotyledons to ensure complete expulsion, as retained placental fragments are a leading cause of postpartum hemorrhage and maternal morbidity in clinical practice.

headings.title: Placental Morphological Variations and Shape Abnormalities
headings.content: Placental morphological variations and shape abnormalities occur when the normal discoid structure deviates during early embryogenesis and placentation. Variations include a bilobate placenta (two equal-sized lobes connected by blood vessels), succenturiate placenta (one or more small accessory lobes developing in the membranes at a distance from the main placenta), and circumvallate placenta (where the chorionic plate is smaller than the basal plate, creating a thick, raised, opaque ring at the margin). These structural anomalies hold profound clinical significance. For instance, a succenturiate lobe can leave behind a retained cotyledon or severed vessels in the lower uterine segment after delivery, triggering severe postpartum hemorrhage. Circumvallate placentas are associated with an increased risk of antepartum bleeding, preterm labor, and placental abruption. For nursing students, recognizing these variations on ultrasound or during postpartum assessment is essential for anticipating complications, educating mothers, and implementing rapid, life-saving interventions in obstetric care units.

headings.title: Abnormalities of Placental Implantation and Insertion
headings.content: Abnormalities of placental implantation and insertion primarily describe where the placenta attaches within the uterine cavity and how the umbilical cord connects to the placental mass. Velamentous cord insertion occurs when the umbilical vessels diverge in the fetal membranes before reaching the placenta, leaving them unprotected by Wharton's jelly and highly vulnerable to rupture, a condition known as vasa previa. If these unprotected vessels cross the internal cervical os, rupture of membranes can lead to rapid fetal exsanguination. Another significant variation is battleore insertion (marginal insertion), where the cord inserts near the edge of the placenta rather than the center. Furthermore, low-lying placentas or placenta previa occur when the placental tissue implants in the lower uterine segment, potentially covering part or all of the internal cervical os. This positional abnormality presents as painless vaginal bleeding in the second or third trimester. Nursing professionals must be vigilant in monitoring patients with these structural deviations, educating them on pelvic rest, and preparing for emergency obstetric interventions.

headings.title: Spectrum of Placenta Accreta and Invasive Placentation
headings.content: The spectrum of placenta accreta and invasive placentation represents a life-threatening obstetric condition characterized by abnormal trophoblastic invasion into the myometrium due to a deficient decidua basalis. This spectrum is traditionally classified into three grades based on depth of invasion: placenta accreta (villi attach directly to the myometrium without invading it), placenta increta (villi invade deep into the myometrium), and placenta percreta (villi penetrate completely through the myometrium and can invade adjacent pelvic organs such as the urinary bladder). Major risk factors include previous cesarean deliveries and uterine curettage, which damage the endometrial-myometrial interface. Diagnosis is increasingly achieved via prenatal ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The primary clinical danger is catastrophic, life-threatening hemorrhage during attempted manual placental removal at delivery. Nursing and multidisciplinary care involves comprehensive preoperative preparation, blood product availability, large-bore intravenous access, and psychological support for the mother, as many cases ultimately necessitate a planned cesarean hysterectomy.

headings.title: Pathological Conditions and Infarctions of the Placenta
headings.content: Pathological conditions and infarctions of the placenta involve degenerative changes that impair the organ's ability to oxygenate and nourish the fetus. Placental infarctions occur when localized areas of maternal blood flow are obstructed, leading to ischemic necrosis of the villi. While small, scattered infarcts are a normal finding in term placentas, extensive infarctions are strongly associated with maternal vascular disorders such as preeclampsia, chronic hypertension, and thrombophilias. Other pathological findings include chorioamnionitis (inflammation of the membranes due to ascending bacterial infection), placental calcifications, and retroplacental hematomas indicative of abruptio placentae. These pathological insults can severely compromise placental reserve, leading to intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), non-reassuring fetal heart rate patterns, oligohydramnios, and stillbirth. For nursing students, understanding these macroscopic and microscopic changes bridges the gap between maternal disease processes and compromised neonatal outcomes, emphasizing the necessity of thorough pathological examination of the placenta following complicated pregnancies.

headings.title: Clinical Presentation and Diagnostic Evaluation
headings.content: Clinical presentation and diagnostic evaluation of placental abnormalities require a combination of careful history taking, physical examination, and advanced imaging technologies. Many structural variations and implantation abnormalities are asymptomatic early in pregnancy and are detected incidentally during routine second-trimester obstetric ultrasound scans. However, conditions like placenta previa and vasa previa commonly present with painless vaginal bleeding, whereas placental abruption presents with painful bleeding and uterine rigidity. Transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasonography are the primary diagnostic modalities, allowing visualization of the lower uterine segment, placental edge, and cord insertion sites. Color Doppler ultrasound is particularly valuable for identifying invasive placentation like placenta accreta, characterized by hypervascular lacunae, as well as confirming vasa previa. In complex cases of suspected invasive placentation, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides superior soft-tissue resolution to gauge the depth of myometrial and parametrial invasion. Nurses play a pivotal role in preparing patients for these diagnostic procedures, explaining what to expect, and promptly reporting abnormal bleeding signs to the attending physician.

headings.title: Maternal and Fetal Complications
headings.content: Maternal and fetal complications arising from placental abnormalities can range from mild antenatal anxiety to life-threatening medical emergencies. Maternal risks are heavily dominated by severe hemorrhage, which can lead to hemorrhagic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), multi-organ failure, and the need for massive blood transfusions or emergency peripartum hysterectomy. Surgical complications are also elevated, particularly ureteral and bladder damage during procedures addressing invasive placentation. Fetal and neonatal risks stem directly from chronic hypoxia, placental insufficiency, and acute asphyxia. These include intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), preterm birth with its associated respiratory distress syndrome, fetal anemia from vasa previa vessel rupture, and intrauterine demise. Nurses caring for these high-risk mothers must maintain high clinical vigilance, frequently monitor vital signs and fetal heart rate patterns, and recognize early indicators of shock or fetal distress to initiate prompt, life-saving multidisciplinary responses.

headings.title: Nursing Management and Collaborative Care
headings.content: Nursing management and collaborative care for patients with placental abnormalities require a proactive, highly coordinated, and multidisciplinary approach involving obstetricians, neonatologists, anesthesiologists, and blood bank personnel. For stable patients with conditions like placenta previa, nursing care includes enforcing pelvic rest (no vaginal examinations or sexual intercourse), monitoring blood loss closely, administering antenatal corticosteroids to promote fetal lung maturity if preterm delivery is anticipated, and ensuring large-bore intravenous access is established. In emergency scenarios involving sudden hemorrhage or abruption, nurses must rapidly initiate standardized hemorrhage protocols, administer oxygen, monitor fluid balance via indwelling urinary catheters, and provide continuous emotional support to the frightened mother and her family. Postpartum care centers on monitoring uterine tone, checking for signs of postpartum hemorrhage or retained fragments, encouraging early bonding when stable, and providing comprehensive discharge education regarding warning signs and follow-up care.
